summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Arts programme returns to 23 Cambridgeshire libraries this autumn
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The Library Presents arts programme returns to Cambridgeshire libraries this autumn. Running from October 16 to December 12, there will be live performances, creative workshops and family events at 23 libraries across the county. Residents curate every event, which ranges from music and theatre to comedy and arts activities, with subsidised tickets available. Alison Whelan, chair of the Communities, Social Mobility and Inclusion Committee at Cambridgeshire County Council, said: "I’m delighted to see the return of The Library Presents which makes high-quality arts and culture events accessible to people across Cambridgeshire through their local libraries at subsidised prices. "These events provide a safe space, a welcoming environment and a sense of community. "I encourage everyone to take a look at the wonderful new autumn and winter event programme to see which fantastic events will be taking place near you." The line-up includes Yiddish music from Klezmer Foygl, award-winning folk from The Bookshop Band and interactive family concerts such as Hat’s Off! It also features immersive digital art, comedy, dance and a sea-shanty singing session at March Library. History fans can hear stories about the women of the Special Operations Executive, while ghost-story workshops will be held in Wisbech and Soham. Hazel Edwards, South East area director at Arts Council England, said: "The Library Presents shows how creativity flourishes when it’s woven into everyday community spaces. "This season’s resident-led programme brings high-quality arts experiences to people of all ages, with a real commitment to inclusion and wellbeing. "And in this National Year of Reading, it’s fantastic to see libraries transformed into places where everyone feels welcome to explore, connect and be inspired." Tickets are on sale online, by phone and at participating libraries, or on the door if available. More information can be found at www.library.live/the-library-presents. Residents helped shape the season by choosing from more than 50 live shows, including music, poetry, dance, digital art and magic.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 'Spectacular' Victorian home in Huntingdon listed on the market for £2.25m
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A "truly spectacular" Victorian home in Huntingdon has been listed on the market for £2.25 million. Located on Thicket Road, the detached house offers six double bedrooms and is described by the listing as "truly spectacular" and "impressively presented". The property’s accommodation is spread over nearly 5,000 sq. ft. and includes four reception rooms and three bathrooms. According to the listing by Carter Jonas, the ground floor features an entrance hall, kitchen/breakfast room, sitting room, dining room, media room, and garden room, as well as a utility room and cloakroom. Impressive – The Victorian home boasts a striking exterior (Image: Zoopla / Carter Jonas) The kitchen is fitted with a "bespoke contemporary kitchen with integrated appliances including an oven, microwave, hob and dishwasher". A central woodburning stove sits between the kitchen and dining areas. The sitting room has an open fireplace and floor-to-ceiling windows that look out on the rear gardens. The first floor includes three bedrooms, two bathrooms, and a cloakroom. Two bedrooms on this floor have fitted wardrobes. Contemporary – The bespoke kitchen features a central island (Image: Zoopla / Carter Jonas) Elegant – Floor-to-ceiling windows fill the spacious sitting room with light (Image: Zoopla / Carter Jonas) The principal bedroom has a dressing area, air conditioning and an en suite with a double-sized shower, bath, “vanity sink unit with stone worktops, WC and heated towel rail”. A further three bedrooms, additional fitted storage, dressing room, and another en-suite are found on the second floor. A detached annexe is included in the listing. This offers a kitchen, sitting room, bathroom, and a first-floor bedroom and dressing room. The listing says the annexe enjoys a courtyard garden "positioned just off the main driveway" and has its own heating system. Contemporary – The bespoke kitchen features a central island (Image: Zoopla / Carter Jonas) Outside, the property is set within grounds measuring close to one acre, with electric timber gates opening to a gravel driveway, described as offering ample parking. There is a double garage and a detached garden studio with a natural stone paved terrace and a hot tub. The gardens are described as predominately lawned and include a paved terrace, mature shrubs, plants, trees, a stable block, and additional store sheds. Expansive – The property sits in grounds measuring close to one acre (Image: Zoopla / Carter Jonas) Permission granted by Zoopla.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Entries open for award showcasing innovative sustainability education
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Entries are open for the East Anglian Clean & Green Awards 2027, including the Educational Trailblazer Award, which is sponsored by East Coast Energy Training Academy. This category will recognise businesses that promote sustainability through education, training or communication. Rachel Bunn, director of the training academy, said she’d be looking for examples of “innovation, collaboration and partnership” to support the education or training of staff or the community. The winner of this award will be able to demonstrate engagement with their audience and the potential for scalability. Rachel Bunn, director of East Coast Energy Training Academy (Image: ECC) Miss Bunn will also be looking for measurable data on skills gained and the learning that has taken place. She said: “The trailblazer will have gone above and beyond the norm and be able to show this through KPIs, evaluation data or outcomes.” This award acknowledges the importance of skills and training in meeting the regional skills needs. “This can be linked to CSR [corporate social responsibility], ESG [environmental, social, and governance] as well as going above and beyond,” she added. “It will raise awareness of your great work to the wider community.” The award will also showcase the great practice of the winning organisation and how education and skills are at the heart of its work. Innovation also plays a key role. It’s something that Miss Bunn said is “at the heart of mixing up skills in the region”. “The ‘do different’ approach should be at the heart of the nomination,” she added. “With the ongoing changes within communities and business, it is vital that employers evolve and create new opportunities.” Submit your entries before the deadline, which is midnight on Sunday, November 8. To enter the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027, please visit cleanandgreenawards.co.uk To find out more about all categories, please click here. East Coast Energy Training Academy is located at East Coast College’s Lowestoft campus. The academy offers a range of commercial training to support the energy and engineering sectors and more. The college facilities are world class and training includes a range of bespoke and qualification models to meet the training needs of the sector as well as those seeking new career opportunities. Courses can support local and international delegates to develop skills as well as competency in areas such as offshore, emergency response, maritime, health and safety, renewable energy, leadership and engineering. The centre also supports bespoke training for sectors to meet evolving training needs and works with employers on new training models such as skills bootcamps and targeted diplomas in the workplace. The judges in this category will be looking for programmes that effectively raise awareness and promote sustainability through education, training or communication. Innovation, engagement and measurable outcomes in knowledge or behaviour change will also be key judging factors. Entries should have the potential for wider reach and scalability.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Ex-Cambs officer drove police vehicle while under the influence of alcohol
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: An ex-Cambridgeshire police officer "put the public at risk" after driving a police vehicle under the influence of alcohol. An accelerated misconduct hearing was held on August 25 at Lysander House, in Bedfordshire, for the former PC Joseph Passby. It was alleged the officer was involved in a crash with a taxi while driving the unmarked vehicle on Trumpington Street, in Cambridge. The incident occurred while the officer was on duty working from Parkside Police Station on June 15. Colleagues attended the scene of the collision and conducted a roadside breath test, the hearing heard. The former officer, who did not attend the hearing, provided a roadside breath sample of 110ug of alcohol per 100 millilitres of breath. Officers initially believed the reading may have been affected by a cough sweet and the use of a vape, according to evidence reviewed by the panel. A further breath test was conducted at the police station where Passby provided a further breath sample of 113ug of alcohol per 100 millilitres of breath. He was arrested on suspicion of driving whilst of the prescribed alcohol limit and taken to Kempston Custody, in Bedfordshire. There he provided two evidential breath specimens reading 88 and 81 microgrammes of alcohol on 100 millilitres of breach. On June 15, Passby was charged with driving a motor vehicle while over the prescribed alcohol limit. He appeared guilty to the offence at Luton Magistrates' Court on July 20 and was sentenced to a 12-month driving disqualification. Passby was found to have breached the standards of discreditable conduct and fitness for duty, amounting to gross misconduct. The allegations were found proven "on the balance of probabilities" with the hearing concluding that had he not previously resigned, the ex-officer would have been dismissed. He will also be placed on the College of Policing's barred list. Chief Constable Simon Megicks said: “Police officers are expected to uphold the law and the highest standards of behaviour. "By driving a police vehicle while on duty and under the influence of alcohol, former PC Passby put the public, colleagues and himself at risk. "His actions were wholly unacceptable and the outcome reflects the seriousness with which we treat conduct that undermines public trust and confidence in policing." summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. More than 27,000 more homes could be built across the Huntingdonshire district as the area faces an ‘unavoidable reality’. Huntingdonshire District Council has approved the latest version of its local plan which highlights where more than 27,000 new homes could be built. The plan will apply until 2046 and was debated on Wednesday evening (September 9). Concerns were raised by residents and parish councillors that the number of new homes planned would essentially create a “new town” without the infrastructure. Under the local plan, more than 27,000 homes could be built in areas including Huntingdon and St Ives. Cllr David Keane said he had grown up in an estate built in the 1960s which had schools, doctors and dentists planned alongside it. The Conservative councillor said: “When I used to talk to older St Ives residents, they remember when all where I was living was fields. “Later I experienced a bit of that myself – the fields I knew disappeared and the landscape changed again. “Most of us don’t particularly like change, unless we’ve chosen it, but there’s one unavoidable reality – we do need homes.” He questioned whether this local plan was the right way to build new homes with infrastructure already strained. He said: “We cannot keep saying that the developer’s pound can be spent here, here and here – it can only be spent once to make this all work”. The plan would aim for 32,200 homes spread over 25 years, of which 4,400 are already built and 11,300 more have been given permission. Cllr Brett Mickelburgh told the council that 18 months ago, the government recognised Huntingdonshire as a “high growth area” and raised their housing target by 50 per cent. The Liberal Democrat councillor said this placed the council in “tilted balance” – where a housing shortfall weighs planning decisions in favour of developers. This means if the council rules against an application, it is more likely to be overruled by a planning inspector who could also order them to pay the developer’s appeal costs. He warned that this could lead to “speculative sites in the wrong places” and urged the council to support the local plan. Cllr Peter Gammons called the number of houses “outrageous” as it would be a 33 per cent increase compared to a national average of between 22 and 25 per cent. The Reform councillor said: “It would be a betrayal of the residents who voted for us and are already angry at the disappearing of their communities.” Cllr Keane said they need confidence not just that infrastructure has been considered but that it can be “realistically delivered” along with the homes. Cllr Alex Bulat said that after some of the “basket-case situations” on the council over the last few months it was “really difficult to find the good will to support the administration on any particular item”. The Labour councillor said: “I understand why residents are opposed to having a lot more new houses and I cannot blame anyone who is rightly questioning this plan. “Especially when they do not see the improvements to infrastructure and local services matching the level of development we have had in our area. “However, it is also true that we haven’t been building enough for decades.” Cllr Lara Davenport-Ray said she believed the target set by the government was “absurdly inflated” but without a local plan the market would decide where homes are built. The Green councillor said the plan was their only safeguard to defend their area “from hostile national planning targets”. Cllr Sarah Conboy, leader of the council, said that voting to support the plan was “not an easy decision” but they were unable to guarantee infrastructure in it. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “We will need to work with government to secure the things that we need government to deliver that we cannot enshrine in a local plan. “If we could guarantee all of the infrastructure first we would do that, but we can’t. “What we will commit to alongside this, though, is lobbying at every opportunity and making the case for Huntingdonshire and what it needs as it continues to grow – now, and for the residents of the future, and that’s something we can promise.” Cllr Mickelburgh said he was “really worried” about hearing a “chicken and egg argument” around infrastructure. He said: “Nobody is going to build a ten million pound water treatment plant upgrade if they don’t know the demand is coming. “You won’t find anyone investing in infrastructure unless they know the demand is coming and the local plan is how they know the demand is coming.” The council voted in favour of the pre-submission with 25 votes for, 17 against and five abstentions.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: First look inside East Cambridgeshire's new crematorium and bereavement centre
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The county's newest crematorium has officially opened its doors with a ribbon-cutting ceremony attended by nearly 200 guests. After nearly eight years, Lake View Bereavement Centre in Mepal is ready to serve East Cambridgeshire—and project leader Cllr Anna Bailey could not be prouder. At Thursday evening’s grand opening, opened by Julie Spence, the Lord Lieutenant of Cambridgeshire, Cllr Bailey beamed as she saw her vision become reality. "I think it is absolutely wonderful; it is so unique and offers a service to the people of East Cambridgeshire that they have so far been missing," said Cllr Bailey. Around 200 people watched as Mrs Julie Spence, Lord Lieutenant of Cambridgeshire, performed the ribbon-cutting to officially open the new Lake View Bereavement Centre at Mepal. (Image: Sarah Cliss) "In the past, if people wanted a cremation, they had to travel outside the district; now they have this wonderful, purpose-built facility, which belongs to the whole community." The £13 million facility stands on the former Mepal Outdoor Centre, which lay derelict for years before becoming a peaceful place for families to say goodbye. Cllr Bailey said some people opposed the project and wanted to save the outdoor centre, but added: "We tried so hard to keep the outdoor centre. We saved it twice, and both times it failed. It got to the stage where the buildings were unsafe and had to come down. "It was being targeted by anti-social behaviour, and we needed to do something with the site, which had been taken over by nature. The chapel in the new bereavement centre can host around 200 people, including standing room. (Image: Sarah Cliss) "In fact, the site has some significant wildlife and plants and is a recognised county nature reserve. We wanted to make use of that to provide an environmentally friendly bereavement centre that took advantage of the beautiful setting, and I think we have achieved that perfectly." Cllr Bailey said the £13 million project was funded by developer contributions, including Community Infrastructure Levy and Section 106 payments, rather than taxpayers. "It has not cost a single taxpayer's penny, and has not landed the council with a debt that needs servicing, and we are proud of that too," said Cllr Bailey. Snow Drop Lodge has a tranquil setting overlooking the water with a large wooden platform for visitors to view nature and the beautiful surroundings. (Image: Sarah Cliss) She said the facility would welcome visitors 365 days a year and generate income for years to come. "I think we have created something very special and unique, and I hope that people will use it and take advantage of this beautiful site - I am just so proud of what has been achieved, and I am grateful to everyone that has been involved in the project," she added. The site can host up to four one-hour funerals a day. There is a garden of remembrance where families can have a plaque to commemorate their loved ones. (Image: Sarah Cliss) "We wanted to ensure people have the time they need to say goodbye with dignity, and not feel pressured or rushed. That is why we will be holding no more than four funerals a day, and there will be an hour in between each one," said Ian Scott-Logan, crematorium and bereavement supervisor. The facility has an all-electric cremator designed to cut emissions. The building has a large multi-faith chapel with floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking trees and water, with room for up to 200 people, including those standing. There is a wooden covered walk way where families can view floral tributes for their loved ones. (Image: Sarah Cliss) A smaller side chapel seats about a dozen people, alongside two family rooms and a small room for people attending funerals from custody. Outside, a covered wooden walkway overlooks the water and gives families a place to display flowers. The site also has a natural burial area that will remain a wildflower meadow, mowed only twice a year. The Snow Drop Lodge can be used by families to hold wakes after funerals, while it can also be used by the community for other small events. (Image: Sarah Cliss) The site also has a pet cemetery for animals from hamsters to horses, but the centre does not offer pet cremations. Families can install remembrance plaques in the memorial garden, beyond which stands Snowdrop Lodge. Snowdrop Lodge is available for funeral wakes and community events. There is a wildflower meadow for natural burials. (Image: Sarah Cliss) Beside the water, Snowdrop Lodge has a large wooden jetty overlooking the site and will host a free bereavement café on the last Saturday of each month at 10.30am; booking is required. Mrs Spence said: "It is a privilege to officially open Lake View Bereavement Centre. "The care and thought that has gone into the design of this beautiful setting is evident throughout. It offers families a peaceful and supportive environment at a time when compassion, dignity and understanding matter most. The grounds are extensive and beautifully set out for visitors to enjoy. (Image: Sarah Cliss) "The centre will undoubtedly become an important place for local communities, not only to remember loved ones but also to find comfort, connection and reflection in its remarkable natural surroundings." Mrs Julie Spence, Lord Lieutenant of Cambridgeshire, gave a speech praising the new facility. (Image: Sarah Cliss) Around 200 people attended the official opening of the new Lake View Bereavement Centre at Mepal on Thursday evening. (Image: Sarah Cliss) Mark Whitten is the crematorium's technician and is in charge of the state-of-the-art electric cremator. (Image: Sarah Cliss) Snow Drop Lodge has a tranquil setting overlooking the water with a large wooden platform for visitors to view nature and the beautiful surroundings. (Image: Sarah Cliss) Mrs Julie Spence, Lord Lieutenant of Cambridgeshire, performed the ribbon-cutting with the help of Cllr Anna Bailey, to officially open the new Lake View Bereavement Centre at Mepal. (Image: Sarah Cliss) Cllr Bailey said: "Lake View belongs to the people of East Cambridgeshire. Whether someone is arranging a funeral, attending one of our bereavement cafés, walking through the memorial gardens or simply finding a moment of peace beside the lake, we hope this will become a valued community asset for generations to come."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The search is on for the region's leading energy champion as entries open for the East of England Energy Ambassador award at the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027. Sponsored by GENERATE, the category celebrates individuals and organisations making a measurable difference through energy innovation, sustainability and leadership, while helping to shape the region's journey towards a net zero future. Judges will be looking for inspiring ambassadors who are influencing others, promoting the sector's strengths and showcasing why the East of England is a powerhouse for energy investment and opportunity The East of England Energy Ambassador award is open to those across all sectors – from clean tech start-ups and large-scale energy providers to educators, engineers, farmers, and local authorities. The award recognises those demonstrating leadership and innovation within their organisation or community. Ian Pease, business development manager of GENERATE (Image: DEPARTURE LOUNGE MEDIA) Ian Pease, business development manager of award sponsor GENERATE, said the judges are looking for “a genuine ambassador for the East of England’s energy sector” who is steering it in a “positive direction”. “I’ve seen firsthand how the composition of the East of England’s energy sector is changing as it continues on its journey to a fully decarbonisation energy system,” he said. “Part of my job is to manage GENERATE, established by local authorities in Norfolk, Suffolk and Essex to attract and support inward investment and business growth in the East of England’s energy sector.” Ian said a true energy ambassador will be a leading figure and role model: a person who consistently goes above and beyond. “We’re looking forward to seeing entries from people who are making a real difference and positive impact to the East of England’s energy sector – people who go out of their way to promote our region’s capabilities and opportunities and why the East is such a great place to do business. “Entering this award will raise awareness of the good work and causes you are supporting, whilst raising your own profile amongst the East of England’s vibrant energy community. “It will also help to reinforce the incredibly important role the East of England’s energy sector plays in both region’s economic well-being and the UK’s energy security and resilience,” Ian added. “Take time with your application and make sure you include all the good work you’re doing – and your plans for the future too.” Submit your entries before the deadline, which is midnight on Sunday, November 8. MEET THE SPONSOR GENERATE connects the East of England to global energy investors by showcasing its unique energy offer, its highly skilled energy supply chain, and its unrivalled centres of innovation, research and science. A partnership of local authorities, GENERATE’s mission is to attract energy-related investment to bring well-paid, highly skilled and sustainable job opportunities to local people and businesses. Since 2021, GENERATE has profiled the region’s investment opportunities, ports and energy supply chain capabilities to national and international audiences. It works to raise awareness of the key infrastructure projects it is developing to support this mission, generating leads and enquiries from supply chain businesses keen to become part of the East of England’s energy sector. AWARD CRITERIA This award recognises a local business or individual who is leading the way in energy innovation, sustainability and leadership, making a measurable difference in the journey toward a net zero future. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Boy's face 'covered in blood' after 'extremely distressing' dog attack in park
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A mother has recalled the harrowing moment her son's face was left "covered in blood" after a dog attack at a Fenland park. Police received a report of the "extremely distressing" attack in Wisbech Park, Lynn Road, Wisbech, at around 6pm on Wednesday (September 9). A 12-year-old boy was injured and taken to hospital for further treatment as officers continue to investigate the incident. Zaneta Kubow, from Wisbech, said her son, Alan, had cycled to the park with a friend to visit a youth club and "hadn't heard from him". "The next thing I know I've got his friend's mum knocking on the door with my son and his friend who went with him," she recalled. "His whole face was covered in blood, his eyebrows were red, so I went to the police and they told me to go straight to A&E." Alan was taken to the Queen Elizabeth Hospital, in King's Lynn, before visiting a plastic surgeon at Norfolk and Norwich Hospital. He received six stitches around his eyebrow and nose and is now under the care of a consultant amid fears the attack could have damaged his nasal bone. "This has been an extremely distressing experience for my son," Ms Kubow added. "He is now terrified and frightened following the attack, and it has understandably had a significant emotional impact on him. "My son is a very active and sporty child and football and boxing are a very important part of his normal life. "Before this incident, he regularly attended football activities at Peterborough United and also played football at Wisbech St Mary Football Club. Ms Kubow revealed that Alan is now no longer able to take part in these activities due to his injuries. "He has been advised to stop his boxing training for approximately three weeks, and he is also unable to participate normally in his football activities while he recovers," she said. "Being unable to attend his usual clubs and activities has therefore affected his normal routine, socialising and enjoyment of everyday life. "He has already been left frightened and traumatised by what happened, and having to stop the activities that he enjoys has made the situation even more difficult for him." Cambridgeshire Police confirmed it has raised a crime of "allowing a dog to be dangerously out of control injuring a person" A spokesperson for the force revealed no arrests have been made and an investigation is ongoing. Those with information or CCTV footage should use reference 35/69822/26 and report it to police online. Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Family says autistic five-year-old is a 'forgotten child' without a school place
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The family of a five-year-old Huntingdon girl are demanding action after authorities failed to find her a school place. Poppy Carter-Till lives minutes from two special needs schools, Prestley Wood Academy in Alconbury and Spring Common in Huntingdon, but has waited nearly 70 weeks for Cambridgeshire County Council to find her a suitable place. Her parents say she has become a “forgotten child”, left without a special needs place despite countless emails, letters and help from a solicitor. Poppy, the youngest of Leisha and Daniel Till’s three children, is autistic and non-verbal and needs more support than a mainstream school can provide. Read more Cambridgeshire council calls on government to deliver promised special needs schools Green light for two new special schools with 270 places Council consult on plans for SEND provision for autistic pupils at school 86-year-old St Neots care home resident fulfils dream with first helicopter flight Woman arrested after 'distraction burglary' in Huntingdonshire town Leisha said the family had met every requirement for a place, but the council still had not found one for Poppy. "We have done everything we can to try to make the process as smooth as possible. We got Poppy an early diagnosis. We have got her an EHCP (Education, Health and Care Plan) in place after seeking a solicitor's help, but still Poppy has been left without a school to go to," said Leisha. Poppy could have started school last September, but her late-summer birthday and additional needs led the family to wait a year, Leisha said. "We kept Poppy back a year, so the council has had an extra year to get this sorted out, but they have failed to do anything," said Leisha. Poppy has been given 15 hours of education outside school, but the sessions are in Cambridge, and the family cannot get her there without neglecting the needs of their other two children, Leisha said. Poppy’s older brother Kai, 17, is autistic and lives in supported accommodation but still relies heavily on his parents. Their middle child, Evelyn, attends mainstream school. "I can't physically get Evelyn to school and be in Cambridge at the same time for Poppy. If I take Evelyn to school, then we will be more than an hour late for Poppy's sessions, which, when she only has 15 hours a week, makes it worthless," said Leisha, who is also balancing work around her children's needs. Leisha and Daniel have both taken jobs at Evelyn’s school to make family life easier, but their income has fallen as a result. Leisha said: "It is just so hard. Poppy is a bright, happy little girl who has so much potential, but she is being denied the chance to fulfil that because Cambridgeshire County Council has not found her a suitable school place. "We have been told that they have approached lots of different special needs schools, and all have said they don't have the capacity to take Poppy, but we have no idea which schools, or why they feel they can't have Poppy. "It is so frustrating; not one person has come out to meet Poppy in person. They are making decisions about a child they haven't even met, based on what's written about her. "If I were to take Poppy or the other children out of school for a holiday, I would be fined or find myself in court. Yet what repercussions are there for a local authority which is failing to provide a child with an education? "It seems there is one rule for them and another for us. Poppy deserves the chance to learn in an environment that is tailored to meet her needs. "We cannot continue to be left waiting without clear answers or meaningful action. Poppy has already been without the education and provision she is entitled to due to failings of the local authority, and we need certainty that we are shown the respect as Poppy’s parents who are fighting for her future that you will listen to us. "We know that Poppy is not alone and there are hundreds of other families in a similar situation to ours, which is why we are speaking out. It's not just to get action for Poppy, but it is to hopefully help stop other families going through what we are going through." A Cambridgeshire County Council spokesperson said: “We are committed to delivering good quality and financially sustainable education placements for all children, including those with SEND, in education settings closer to home. “The continued increase in demands for Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) over the last few years, in line with national trends, has led to significant pressure on in-county specialist placements creating uncertainty for families, like the Tills, and is driving up costs. “In some cases, we are still consulting with schools on the most appropriate placements for children for September 2026 entry. Unfortunately, these consultations cannot progress during school holidays, while schools are closed. “The council is working with the Department for Education to bring forward new in-county specialist provisions as soon as possible “We commission quality assured Alternative Provisions for students with EHCP’s that are unable to access mainstream education, while waiting for a suitable special school place to be allocated. Alternative provisions may include online and in-person learning, tutoring or therapeutic interventions.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 10 high-rise buildings in Cambridgeshire and Peterborough still have unsafe cladding
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Nearly 10 years on from the Grenfell Tower fire, ten high-rise buildings in Cambridgeshire and Peterborough still have unsafe cladding, but the combined authority say they are “confident” it will be removed in time to meet government targets. In a performance report given to the combined authority’s overview and scrutiny panel, it was noted that four residential buildings have had their cladding or flammable insulation partially or fully replaced. This included three high-rise buildings, of seven stories or more, and one medium-rise building defined as having five or six stories. This was the same number of buildings with unsafe cladding replaced as the last time the figures were brought to panel in June. The report noted that it is “ultimately the responsibility of building owners” to make sure that “risks have been identified and necessary action taken”. It said that “very good progress has been maintained” and the authority is “on track to carry out all necessary assessments and engagement with landlords” to meet their targets. Out of the region’s 34 high-rise residential buildings – 21 require no further action but ten still need to have their cladding replaced. Cllr Anna Bradnam, of South Cambridgeshire District Council, said she was “very glad to see” buildings assessed and fixed but “slightly concerned” that ten still hadn’t. The Liberal Democrat councillor asked what was being done to monitor them. Daniel Buckridge, performance and evaluation manager, said he had been advised that Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service had written to the owners “to check on their progress or what their plans are for remediation”. He said there had been an issue with the government sharing details of buildings that had joined the national cladding scheme, but when given access they would be able to “get progress updates on those directly from that system”. He said: “Once we have that, we’ll have a better understanding of what’s going to be delivered when and we’ll be able to then perhaps set targets for when we expect those remediations to be complete.” Cllr Bradnam said: “I don’t know how many years we are on now from Grenfell tower, but writing a letter to the landowners seems a relatively mild thing to be doing. This is something that, actually it was quite some time after that, but the requirement came in that unsafe cladding should be removed”. Mr Buckridge said the target for cladding to be removed is December 31, 2029 for high-rise buildings and December 31, 2031 for medium rise buildings. These deadlines were introduced in July 2025. Of Cambridgeshire and Peterborough’s 144 medium-rise residential buildings, 59 needed no further action and 84 must have their cladding replaced. He said: “We’re working with resources that have been passed on to us, but this wasn’t previously a duty for combined authorities. We are confident that we’re going to meet those targets.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Plans to ‘reimagine’ bus services across Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Changes to bus services across Cambridgeshire have been outlined with alterations to 31 services listed. A report outlined a number of changes to the public transport system, with some stops dropped off routes, timetables altered and other services added. Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority’s transport committee met on Wednesday (September 9) to note changes to bus services. The committee was given a report titled “Bus Services Reimagined” detailing the proposed final changes across the region. They did not have the final say on the plans, but were instead asked to vote on whether to recommend their approval to the combined authority’s board. Cllr Lorna Dupré, representing Cambridgeshire County Council, said she was “grateful for the honesty in the title” as “for too many communities it means the replacement of bus services with imaginary ones”. The Liberal Democrat councillor said that cuts to services were made necessary by the mayor’s decision not to increase the mayoral precept and divert funds “to subsidise car parking”. Paul Bristow was elected mayor of the combined authority in 2025 under the pledge not to increase the mayoral precept and avoid significant borrowing during his term. A report on bus franchising, which was approved under the previous mayor, warned earlier this year that Cambridgeshire bus services could be cut by more than a third in the next decade without additional funding. The Conservative mayor also promised to introduce free parking at council-owned car parks, with £1.5m allocated in his budget over two years to bring the policy to Peterborough and Huntingdonshire. Cllr Dupré said if residents aren’t sure if the bus they want to take will still be running in six months, they will “stop even considering public transport as an option”. She highlighted “losses for people” in the report – noting the 65 service will no longer stop in Buckden to bring residents to their GP. She said the Tiger On Demand service, which can be booked to stop at specific bus stops, is being used to “fill in gaps”. Labour councillor Angus Ellis, representing Peterborough City Council, said: “This should be bus services reduced, rather than reimagined”. Cllr Tim Bick, representing Cambridge City Council, said the combined authority needs to work harder at encouraging bus usage before axing services for low use if they are “serious about reimagining bus services”. The Liberal Democrat councillor noted the T2 and T3 buses, designed to link the peripheries of Cambridge without going through the centre, both of which will be replaced. He said: “We’re going to have to try harder to change behaviour in order to get the usage for a service like that. “If we want to do bigger things – we need to stick with change and support it.” If approved by the combined authority’s board, in February 2027 the first stage of changes would be made to bus services. In Fenland, services 56 and T7 will be redesigned to “keep important links” with the report stating links between March and Wisbech “would improve” with earlier and later journeys and better weekend provision. Timetables for the services 46 and 50 could change, including connections through Chatteris and revised times for Wisbech villages. In Huntingdonshire, the T12 would be withdrawn with improvements made to the 301 service between St Ives, Earith and Somersham. The 65 service would no longer stop at Buckden and would serve St Neots Rail Station, extending from the Offords to Godmanchester, the Hemingfords and St Ives. In Cambridge, the 8 to Hilton would extend to St Ives and combine with the 69 to “offer more links to communities”. The T4 between Addenbrooke’s and Newmarket would see a timetable and route change in Cambridge and Little Wilbraham to “improve punctuality”. The next stage would happen in August 2027, with several existing services in South and East Cambridgeshire serving Haverhill and the Newmarket area replaced with new services 119, 120 and 121 to make the network simpler. The 26 towards Royston would be increased to an hourly service, no longer serving Foxton, and extending to Guilden Morden every two hours. In South Cambridgeshire, new 27, 27A and 27H services would be introduced to replace parts of the services 7A, 17, 114 and T3. The 75 would be improved to provide hourly links to Cambridge and the T5 would have reliability and coordination improvements, including new evening journeys. The T2 service will be replaced by a new route from Cambridge North to Darwin Green, Eddington and the east of Cambridge city centre. In Peterborough, services 60 and 61 would be merged and there would be “minor changes” to the timetables of services 62 and 63.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Award shines a light on sustainability strategies that deliver
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Businesses prioritising their environmental impact are encouraged to enter the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027. The Sustainability Strategy Award recognises organisations that are turning sustainability ambitions into practical action, delivering measurable environmental benefits while creating a framework for long-term progress. Category sponsor Opergy believes the strongest strategies are those that can demonstrate not just vision, but delivery. Johnathan Reynolds, managing director of Opergy Group, will be looking for evidence that sustainability is embedded within a business. “We are likely to be most impressed by strategies that are ambitious but practical, rooted in evidence and clearly connected to the organisation’s core purpose,” he said. “The specific theme matters less than the quality of the strategy. We want to see clear baselines, prioritised actions, accountable leadership, realistic investment and measurable results – including honest recognition of trade-offs, constraints and what still needs to be done.” Johnathan Reynolds, managing director of Opergy Group (Image: Opergy) For Mr Reynolds, entering the category is also an opportunity for organisations to take stock of their achievements and assess the effectiveness of their sustainability efforts. “The process should help organisations bring together their evidence, test whether ambitions are matched by delivery and recognise the contribution of colleagues and partners,” he said. Stakeholder engagement will be another area of focus for the category judges. “Sustainability challenges rarely sit within the control of a single organisation,” said Mr Reynolds. “Evidence of meaningful collaboration therefore tells us that an entrant understands the system in which its strategy has to work.” The entry deadline for the Sustainability Strategy Award is midnight on Sunday, November 8. For more information about the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027, please visit cleanandgreenawards.co.uk To read about all of the award categories, please click here. Opergy is a strategic advisory and delivery partner working across energy, infrastructure, sustainability and regional growth. From its headquarters in East Anglia and teams across the UK, the firm helps businesses, public bodies and major projects turn complex challenges into clear, deliverable strategies. Opergy’s work spans clean energy, infrastructure, skills, supply chains, investment, decarbonisation and place-based economic development. It combines evidence-led research, sector expertise and practical delivery support to help clients make better decisions, build stakeholder confidence and create measurable impact. The judges will be seeking a project or strategy that excels in reducing or offsetting carbon emissions. Innovation, measurable carbon reductions and the potential for the strategy to be scaled or replicated elsewhere will be key factors. Collaboration with stakeholders will strengthen the entry.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Primark shoppers set for major change as delivery plans revealed
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Shoppers are celebrating as Primark is planning to launch home delivery in Great Britain for the first time. The high street giant has traditionally focused heavily on its huge network of physical stores, but that is now changing as it looks to expand its online offering. Primark's owner, Associated British Foods (ABF), has bought a new warehouse in Sheffield to support the move. However, shoppers will have to wait for now, as the company has not revealed exactly when home delivery will launch. ABF said the service would come “in the future”. The move comes as Primark continues to expand its click and collect service, allowing customers to browse and buy selected items online before collecting them from stores. The new home delivery service could give shoppers another way to get their Primark purchases without having to make a trip to the high street. ABF said Primark's UK business had continued to perform better than some of its other markets. Like-for-like sales across the retailer are expected to have fallen by 2.6% over the financial year, which ends on Saturday, compared with the previous year. The biggest weakness was in continental Europe, while UK sales are estimated to have edged up by 0.6%. Primark said sales got off to a strong start during the summer, but the prolonged hot weather affected demand for autumn clothing as shoppers delayed buying their new-season wardrobes. Trading has improved in recent weeks as temperatures have cooled, the company said. Recommended reading George Weston, chief executive of ABF, said: “Our priority focus areas, the UK and womenswear, continued to outperform our other markets and categories. “Primark has made significant progress in building its digital capabilities and will continue this through both growing click & collect and by offering home delivery in Great Britain in the future. “There is now an opportunity for incremental and profitable growth through this channel.”

The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Huntingdonshire District Councillors unanimously backed a review of money spent on plans to develop three car parks at a full council meeting on September 9. Property developer Capital & Centric wants to build major housing developments on three car parks in partnership with HDC in St Neots, St Ives and Huntingdon. No planning application has been submitted, but residents are already angry at the prospect of losing large car parks in the three towns. St Neots residents turned out to a public consultation on the controversial development Councillors raised the issue at a full council meeting at Pathfinder House in Huntingdon on September 9. Councillor Ryan Coogan called on the council to fully withdraw from the Capital & Centric project and review the scheme and money already spent. Cllr Ryan Coogan More than £1 million has been spent on early-stage design and planning work, it was revealed in a document released by the council this week. Total costs claimed by Capital & Centric between January and July 2026 amount to £1,058,720. The biggest item was £323,751.42 in architectural fees. The figures also included more than £200,000 in development management fees and £100,000 in project management costs. Councillor Ross Martin challenged the spending at the meeting. Cllr Ross Martin He said: "Over a million pounds has been spent so far. On what? "I don't know and our residents don't know. "How on earth has it cost that much to do a pre-application on three sites? "It doesn't make sense." There was debate between councillors at the meeting over an amendment to the motion, which saw it reduced from four pages to just two. Cllr Coogan called it "an amendment that negates the motion" and clashed with chairman Cllr Stephen Ferguson. However, the amendment was passed by 28 votes to 18. All 46 councillors present then backed the new motion to examine the spending. The council's joint administration had already collapsed over the proposals, after Green councillors quit the Liberal Democrat-led coalition citing how they were handled.

The event will run from 4pm to 7pm on Tuesday, September 15, at Hartford Village Hall, according to a letter sent to neighbours by Royal Pilgrim Communications for Lidl. The letter reads: "We're now holding a drop-in event to share further details and gather your feedback ahead of submitting a planning application." Leaflets and a freepost feedback form were sent out to gather residents’ initial views on the draft plans. The proposed Lidl would be built on land south of Main Street (B1514) and west of Huntingdon Road. Aerial photos show the site of the planned supermarket. The site is located within travelling distance of Hartford, St Ives, Wyton and Houghton (Image: Geoff Soden) A drop in session will be held on September 15 (Image: Geoff Soden) It would be located within easy travel of Hartford and the surrounding villages of Houghton, Wyton and St Ives. The store would have a 1,343 sq m sales area, a bakery and 118 parking spaces, including bays for disabled people and parents with children. It would also have two electric vehicle charging spaces, with room for more in future. Project team members will attend the session to answer residents’ questions. A planning application has not yet been submitted; the site previously had outline approval for 25 to 30 homes, but that scheme was not progressed. Councillor Nathan Hunt said residents had raised concerns about the Main Street junction, site landscaping and flood risk.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Progress update on £329m A141 and St Ives transport scheme
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A major transport package for Huntingdon and St Ives has moved closer to delivery, with its Outline Business Case nearing completion. The update was presented to the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority's transport committee on Wednesday. The A141 and St Ives Improvements Study aims to improve transport links along the A141 corridor and around Huntingdon and St Ives. The scheme aims to make journeys more reliable, strengthen the road network and support housing and economic growth across Huntingdonshire. What the package is looking like. (Image: CPCA) The report says the project fits both the Combined Authority's Local Transport and Connectivity Plan and Huntingdonshire District Council's emerging Local Plan. The plans identify the North Huntingdon Growth Cluster as a major development area, with potential for around 15,000 homes and 15,000 jobs by 2046. The package includes a bypass linking Spittals Interchange to a new B1090 roundabout, extra capacity on Harrison Way in St Ives, Park and Ride sites at Huntingdon Racecourse and Wyton Airfield, and new bus services linking Huntingdon, St Ives, Wyton and Alconbury Weald. Walking and cycling improvements are also a major part of the plans. A map showing the proposed routes. (Image: CPCA) They include two off-road routes between Huntingdon and St Ives, segregated paths alongside the A1123 and Harrison Way, and A141 improvements including a new East Coast Main Line crossing. The report says the plans have already changed after public consultation, with the proposed Meadow Lane bus gate and A1123 right-turn ban onto Needingworth Road dropped and walking and cycling routes revised. The package is estimated to cost £328.6 million, while modelling suggests it would deliver "high value for money", with a benefit-cost ratio above two under a high-growth scenario. The Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority's transport committee was given an update on the progress of the A141 and St Ives improvements study at its meeting this week. (Image: CPCA) Work on the Full Business Case is expected to begin this autumn, with surveys and early design continuing until spring 2027. The Full Business Case is scheduled for development between summer 2027 and summer 2028, but funding has yet to be secured. The Combined Authority said it would keep exploring funding options, including government support and developer contributions. Earlier consultation material identified road-safety concerns, poor noise and air quality, and drivers "rat-running" through villages on minor roads as issues the scheme aims to address.

The Behaviour Change Campaign of the Year award, sponsored by Clarksons Port Services, celebrates campaigns that have successfully encouraged more sustainable behaviours and delivered a positive environmental impact. Adam Tucker, account manager at Clarksons Port Services, is looking forward to seeing entries that demonstrate genuine and measurable change. “We want to recognise initiatives that inspire people to take action and create lasting, positive behaviour change in support of sustainability,” said Mr Tucker. He explained that the strongest submissions will combine creativity with evidence, demonstrating how innovative ideas, audience insight and effective engagement have influenced behaviours in meaningful ways. “We’re particularly interested in campaigns that not only capture attention but also motivate people to adopt more sustainable habits,” he said. Adam Tucker, account manager at Clarksons Port Services (Image: Clarksons Port Services) Mr Tucker believes behaviour change plays a vital role in addressing environmental challenges and achieving long-term sustainability goals. “While innovation, technology and policy all have an important role to play, lasting environmental improvements ultimately depend on the decisions people make every day,” he said. “Successful sustainability initiatives don’t just inform people; they inspire and enable action.” Innovation and audience engagement will also be important judging criteria, alongside the potential for ideas to be scaled or adapted more widely. Mr Tucker added: “The ability to scale, adapt and inspire change across different communities or sectors is an important part of creating long-term environmental impact. “We’re excited to celebrate the organisations leading the way and recognising campaigns that have the potential to make a difference well beyond their original scope.” The entry deadline for the Behaviour Change Campaign of the Year award is midnight on Sunday, November 8. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: MP wades in amid claims migrants being housed in Huntingdonshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary:
An MP has waded in and called for improved communication amid claims migrants are being housed in a Huntingdonshire town. The call follows a statement from government contractor Serco over rumours that asylum seekers were being moved into empty flats in Eynesbury, St Neots. A video shared with The Hunts Post appears to show a housing officer from Serco inspecting the properties on August 13. It is understood the official "confirmed" asylum seekers will move into the addresses, although this could not be independently verified. Concerns have been raised about the suitability of the properties, which are located in close proximity to vulnerable residents. This newspaper has chosen not to identify the exact location of the properties to ensure the safety of those who may live there. The MP for St Neots and Mid Cambridgeshire, Ian Sollom, confirmed Serco submitted a nomination for the properties on May 6 this year. This was assessed by "three separate council teams before being supported for family use", he told this newspaper. "What clearly didn't happen is any communication with residents, ward councillors, or me as the local MP," he said. "Finding out about something like this from social media, rather than from any official source, is a bad way to learn what's happening on your own street, and I don't think raising questions about that makes anyone unreasonable." According to Mr Sollom, the Home Office confirmed on August 20 that four family properties had been procured but were not occupied at that time. He urged locals to treat any claims about current occupancy status "with some caution until they're confirmed by the Home Office directly". However, the MP revealed he has seen figures that "don't match what I've been told directly by the Home Office - for instance, the number of properties involved". "That may not be deliberate misinformation," he explained. "It could simply be a symptom of how little official information has reached residents, which is itself part of the problem." Read more Government contractor responds to claims migrants being housed in Hunts
    Reform councillor tables motion to stop further asylum accommodation in Hunts
    LIVE: Cambs leaders react as government halt LGR decisions
    Photos show large turnout at first Capital & Centric consultation in Hunts
    WATCH: 'Disgusting' car park plans slammed by St Neots residents at consultation Moving forward, Mr Sollom said he'd like to see the local authority and representatives "properly looped in before a property is brought into use". "I'd like the Home Office to communicate directly with affected communities rather than leaving residents to find out secondhand," he added. "The contractual process with the council doesn’t include any public-facing communication, and that's the gap I want closed." Councillor Stephen Ferguson said the wider community had not "been given the information they need to plan ahead". He added: "The priority now is for Serco, the council, the police, local services, community groups and residents to work together. "We need to keep everyone safe, make sure the right plans are in place and give people clear facts instead of leaving rumours to spread." "St Neots is a strong and welcoming community. If we share the facts, speak calmly and work together, we can deal with this in a sensible and responsible way." Serco said it does not confirm the addresses of properties it may rent for asylum accommodation. A spokesperson said: "We work under the direction of the Home Office, who decide where people are placed, based on overall national demand." Despite this, Cambridgeshire Constabulary said it had "been notified by partners and are engaging with them". Huntingdonshire District Council said it was aware of "speculation" regarding "potential asylum accommodation in the Eynesbury ward of St Neots". A spokesperson said: "Decisions about asylum accommodation are the responsibility of the Home Office and its accommodation providers. "While the council may be consulted and can raise local concerns where appropriate, it does not make these decisions. "It would not be appropriate for the council to comment on, verify, or speculate about reports relating to specific properties or individuals. They added: "Any confirmation should come from the Home Office or the relevant accommodation provider. "We encourage residents to rely on trusted, official sources and avoid sharing unverified information." Have you got a story you want to share? The reception also thanked the organisations that supported the region’s presence at UKREiiF. Shaun Grady, chairman of the business board, said: "It's a really exciting time as Cambridgeshire and Peterborough is making a larger impact across the UK. "Next year is going to be even bigger and better with business propositions for development partners, to exploit the enormous potential that exists here in our region." summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 18 prisoners to be released early in Bedfordshire next month
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Eighteen offenders are due for early release in Bedfordshire next month as part of a national programme to ease pressure on prison space, a meeting heard. The probation service will supervise them within the county and is confident it can manage the situation, despite its financial constraints, the Bedfordshire Police and Crime Panel was told. “This has been the county force’s busiest summer for a long time, with significant increases in incidents and cases,” according to Bedfordshire Police and Crime Commissioner John Tizard. “We’ve had a fatal police shooting (in Bedford), a rail crash (near Elstow), five homicides, the process of extraditing the Tate brothers from the United States, and extraditing the suspect from South Africa in respect of one of the homicides,” he explained. “There’ve been a number of other incidents too, as well as the Bedford River Festival which took 150 officers. We’ve 80-plus county lines and a significant number of organised crime syndicates. “The pressures have been quite significant. It’s no excuse for performance, but it’s putting all this into that perspective.” He described the early release of prisoners as having been “a moving position”, saying: “We now know 18 prisoners will be released early in Bedfordshire in October. “They’re known and named, and the probation service will have responsibility for their supervision. The police will be informed of those releases. It puts pressure on the offender management unit. “If there’s a level of recall, the police often have to get involved. The probation service is confident it can manage the position, but it also has resource restraints. “Early release is probably inevitable given the current state of the prison estate across the country. Even if you build new prisons, you can’t build them at the pace required.” There are some areas of significant challenge in terms of overall performance in Bedfordshire, “although we’re moving in the right direction in aspects such as responding to the public”, added the PCC. “The police are consistently achieving 90 per cent and often above of 999 calls answered within ten seconds, which is the national standard. The bigger challenge is getting to ‘immediate cases’, which should be within 15 minutes and where the national standard is 80 per cent plus. “We’re currently well below that. We’re making progress and are in the high 50s (per cent) on a regular basis now, but that has to improve. “Another area is solving crime. A new report says investigating crime is an issue on a national basis. That’s partly because there are insufficient qualified detectives. “Bedfordshire has more of these than a year ago and quite a considerable number in training. The solve rate is better than it was, but there’s still some way to go. “Domestic abuse and domestic violence are a priority and very much a target for the police. We’re making significant improvements in that area, but there’s some way to go. “It’s the repeat offences. We’re using the orders available through the courts to hold the perpetrators to account. That’s an area of great focus.” Asked about progress on police reform, Mr Tizard replied: “The government’s intention is to replace PCC’s with a new form of governance from May 2028. “The ambition is that mayors would take over the role. The Police Reform Bill was due to be presented to Parliament within the last two weeks. “But that’s not happened and the expectation is this legislation won’t be presented for its first reading until January. The government is still saying it aims to achieve the same timetable, although it’s a tight schedule.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Controversial guided busway approved for Cambs
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The government has approved plans for a controversial new busway linking Cambridge and Cambourne. The Cambourne to Cambridge guided busway route, known as C2C, was first proposed in 2014 with a two-month public inquiry finishing in November of last year. There were concerns about safety after the deaths of three people on a different busway in the county between 2015 and 2021. The project is estimated to cost £180m and will run through the century-old Coton Orchard, and has led to more than 300 objections to the route. The plans will be delivered by Cambridgeshire County Council on behalf of the Greater Cambridge Partnership (GCP). The planned route will go via the new Bourn Airfield development, Hardwick, Coton and the university’s Cambridge West site. The GCP said Cambourne is expected to grow “significantly” over the next few years, with plans for up to 13,000 new homes, and hope the busway will provide 10,000 daily passenger trips. The secretary of state approved the plans on Tuesday evening (September 8). Cllr Brian Milnes, chair of the the GCP’s executive board, said that with thousands more homes planned for Cambourne, the route will be a “desperately needed new transport link”. He said: “We all know how difficult it can be for residents to get from Cambourne into Cambridge. “Whilst many objectors wanted Cambourne to Cambridge to take a different route, almost all of them agreed that improved public transport is essential for our area.” Cllr Lucy Nethsingha, leader of Cambridgeshire County Council, said the link would give “tens of thousands of residents” easy access to “low carbon and low congestion transport into Cambridge city”. Cllr Katie Thornburrow, leader of Cambridge City Council, said the route was an “important component” of an “integrated transport solution for the region”. She said: “Offering fast, efficient public transport along with options for active transport like cycling gives everyone more choice. “I am confident this scheme will ease congestion and delays on key routes into the city, improve journey reliability and contribute to better air quality, while supporting sustainable growth for communities both now and in the future.” Cllr Bridget Smith, leader of South Cambridgeshire District Council, said: “It’s vital our growing communities have a reliable, sustainable, and affordable way to travel between Cambourne and the city – giving them a genuine alternative to driving. “It will be particularly transformational for younger residents – giving them better access to Cambridge’s opportunities.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New independent veterinary practice opens in Huntingdon
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A new independent veterinary practice has opened in Huntingdon. Huntsbridge Vets welcomed its first clients to its new independent practice at Vantage Park on Tuesday, September 1. This followed a community open day and ribbon-cutting ceremony attended by MP Ben Obese-Jecty. The practice is the result of months of planning and preparation by its four founders, who bring together expertise in veterinary medicine, nursing, management and client care. Julie Eastham, practice manager and one of the founding partners, said: "It has been a huge amount of work bringing our vision for Huntsbridge Vets to life, so seeing the practice open and welcoming our first clients has been incredibly special. Huntsbridge Vets opens its doors in Huntingdon this week (Image: Huntsbridge Vets) "Our open day gave us the opportunity to meet many of the people who will become our clients, but now it’s even more exciting to actually welcome them and their pets through the doors. "Building those relationships and getting to know our clients and their animals is one of the things we have been looking forward to most." The founding team also includes veterinary surgeons Nigel Belgrove and Rachael Day, and registered veterinary nurse Anne Selfe. They say their goal is to provide high-quality veterinary care in a practice that is genuinely connected to the community. Huntsbridge Vets is now open to new clients and pets (Image: Huntsbridge Vets) Huntsbridge Vets has been designed with a modern, welcoming feel, aiming to combine contemporary facilities with a personal approach. Mr Belgrove said: "We have a really passionate team, and we all share the same ambition for Huntsbridge Vets. "We want to provide excellent clinical care, but just as importantly, we want people to feel that they know who is looking after their pets and that they have a veterinary team they can trust." MP Ben Obese-Jecty attends ribbon-cutting at Huntingdon practice (Image: Huntsbridge Vets) Ms Day said the environment was designed with comfort in mind. She said: "Visiting the vets can be stressful for both pets and their owners. Founders Anne, Julie, Nigel and Rachael welcome first clients (Image: Huntsbridge Vets) "We have tried to create an environment that is calm, welcoming and reassuring, while ensuring that we can provide the high standard of veterinary care our patients deserve."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Campaign urges Cambs people to talk openly to help prevent suicide
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The STOP Suicide campaign is urging people across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough to spot the signs someone is struggling and start supportive conversations. Ashley Bunn, chief executive of CPSL Mind, said: "On World Suicide Prevention Day, and every day, we must continue to raise awareness about suicide and support people to have open and supportive conversations. "Our new strategy outlines how too many people still only reach support at the point of crisis. "We will continue to work tirelessly to improve access to timely and accessible support in the community, ensuring people access the right support at the right time for them." Denver (Image: Cambridge United Foundation) Led by CPSL Mind and backed by NHS and public health teams, the campaign urges people to spot warning signs, ask directly about suicide and help those at risk stay safe. It highlights that one in four people will experience suicidal thoughts during their lifetime. Fenland has the highest reported suicide rate in Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, while Peterborough’s rate is also above the national average. STOP Suicide is sharing personal stories from people who have faced mental health challenges, including Dee from St Neots. In the campaign video, Dee said: "When you go through something so dark and so isolating, there is no hope. "I felt like there was no other solution, I was so ready to end it all." A conversation with a friend’s father changed her perspective, and she hopes the campaign shows others that even a glimpse of hope is possible. STOP Suicide workshops are available to help individuals recognise warning signs, ask about suicide, and support others to stay safe. Find resources and information at www.cpslmind.org.uk. Anyone facing an immediate emergency should call 999, while the Samaritans can be contacted on 116 123 for emotional support.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Entries are now open for the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027, including the Apprentice of the Year, sponsored by RenewableUK. This category celebrates the rising stars helping to shape a more sustainable future, recognising individuals who have demonstrated exceptional commitment and development throughout their apprenticeship. Elizabeth Conboy, executive director, commercial of RenewableUK is looking for entries that show apprentices making the most of the opportunities available to them while delivering benefits for their organisation. She said: “I hope to see submissions from nominees who can evidence professional development and learning milestones.” Elizabeth Conboy, executive director, commercial at RenewableUK (Image: RenewableUK) Ms Conboy said the award provides an opportunity to celebrate the role apprentices play in driving innovation, skills development and business success. She said: “For apprentices, it offers valuable recognition and helps raise their profile within the industry. “For employers, it showcases their commitment to nurturing talent, investing in future leaders and building the diverse, skilled workforce needed to deliver a more sustainable future.” Discussing the impact the accolade could have, Ms Conboy said: “For the winner and finalists, I hope it will boost confidence, raise their profile, open new career opportunities and strengthen professional networks. “It also highlights the importance of apprenticeships, inspiring others to develop their skills and pursue leadership roles in the transition to a sustainable energy future.” She said exceptional apprentices stand out from their peers with their attitude, curiosity and adaptability. “Outstanding apprentices combine curiosity, initiative and a willingness to learn,” she said. “In a fast-moving sector like renewables, those who demonstrate adaptability, collaboration and a genuine passion for making a positive impact are the ones who truly stand out.” Submit your entries before the deadline, which is midnight on Sunday, November 8. To enter the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027, please visit cleanandgreenawards.co.uk To find out more about all categories, please click here. RenewableUK is the UK’s leading trade association for the renewable energy sector, representing close to 500 members spanning the full supply chain, including offshore wind, onshore wind, energy storage, and wave and tidal power. RenewableUK exists to create and protect the political, commercial and public conditions needed to accelerate the UK’s clean energy transition. The trade association works on behalf of its members to demonstrate that renewable energy delivers energy security, lower bills, investment, jobs and economic growth, while helping remove the barriers that prevent deployment at scale. By connecting industry and policy makers, RenewableUK strengthens the nation’s global leadership in renewables, building a secure, affordable and sustainable energy future. The judges will be looking for an apprentice who has demonstrated exceptional commitment, achievement and personal development. The winner should showcase a strong work ethic, a passion for learning and a positive contribution to their workplace, colleagues and the wider business. Evidence of growth, initiative and the ability to overcome challenges will be key judging factors.

Building on the success of the 2026 awards, this year’s programme reaffirms our commitment to recognising and rewarding those who are making a real difference – whether through innovation, education, energy efficiency, biodiversity protection, or sustainable business practices. Whether you’re a non-profit running a recycling drive, a start-up tackling waste reduction, or a school leading a biodiversity project, this is your chance to showcase your work and inspire others. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A person has died after a crash in which a car left the road near a Bedfordshire village. Emergency services were called the incident between Hill Lane and Southill Road near Upper Caldecote at around 8.30pm on Friday (September 4). A person was tragically pronounced dead at the scene and police are now appealing for help in establishing the events leading up the collision. Sergeant Mark Atkins from the Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Hertfordshire Roads Policing Unit, said: "We’re appealing for witnesses following a single vehicle collision which has sadly left one person dead. "Please check your dash-cam footage and get in touch to help us establish what caused this collision."
